4.5 — The Jump: Getting the Player Off the Ground

The cave is the first place in this game where down means something. Walk off the edge of the floor and you do not fall — you keep walking, level. Today you turn gravity back on for one scene, and use the same body to throw the character into the air.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make the player jump in the cave?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

The player should leap off the ground in the cave, and right now nothing in this project can do it. The body you built in 2.1 has Gravity Scale 0, so the cave has no down; and no line in PlayerController.cs has ever pushed the player up. "Make the player jump" is two mechanisms wearing one name: a world that pulls you down, and one instant that spends that pull.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the Player a body that falls in this sceneBody Type Dynamic and Gravity Scale above zero - it takes both. Gravity Scale multiplies the project gravity Physics 2D holds at -9.81 on Y. Your body has been Dynamic at Gravity Scale 0 since 2.1, because a top-down character who obeys gravity walks off the edge of the world.Read: the rb.gravityScale row of the quick reference.
  2. Tell the script which world it woke up inThe same Player prefab is played in both worlds, so "am I in the cave?" is a fact about the scene: one serialized bool, ticked on the cave copy and left alone on the hub copy - the same field shape you have used since 1.3, pointed at the world instead of at the player.Read: the [SerializeField] private row in the quick reference, and the field rules from 1.3.
  3. Turn gravity on once, when the scene loadsA gated write in Start(): if the flag is on, hand the body a gravity scale. Once, before the first frame - in Update() the same number is written sixty times a second for a value that never changes.Read: the void Start() row of the quick reference.
  4. Notice one press of the jump keyInput.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) inside the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4. It is true on the single frame the key goes down; Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space) is true on every frame it is held - a jump is a moment, not a state.Read: the Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) row of the quick reference, and the input functions from 1.4.
  5. Hand the body one upward flick, and let gravity spend itAddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse): one instant change in momentum. The height is the impulse divided by mass, the rise is paid for by the gravity from part 1, and the apex is the frame the vertical velocity reaches zero.Read: the rb.AddForce(... ForceMode2D.Impulse) row of the quick reference.

Two of those five parts are new to this course, and they are the two that make a jump: a number that changes momentum in one instant, and a world that spends it. The other three are work you have already done - a Dynamic body is 2.1, a serialized field is 1.3, a key check is 1.4 - which is why this lesson can hand you every line and still be worth the hour. The new part is one call; the work is choosing where it goes.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the player jump" cannot be looked up - there is no such API. "Push a rigidbody upward once" can, and the answer is one line long.

Your turn

Parts two and three are the same trick as every Inspector checkbox since 1.3: a field holds a fact, and code reads it. What fact about the scene - not about the player - does the flag hold, and where would you look to prove it is ticked?

Nothing in the jump code measures time, and yet the arc has a height. Where does the height come from, and which part would you change first if the jump felt wrong?

The flick is spent in one frame, but the rise takes about half a second. Which part of the five is doing the work in the frames where no key is pressed?

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Project window → open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity — the cave — then Game view → press Play and walk off the edge of the floor. Nothing falls, and that is not a bug: the Rigidbody2D you gave the Player in 2.1 has Gravity Scale 0, because a top-down character who obeys gravity falls through the world forever. You were right then. The cave is the first place where you are wrong.
  2. Hierarchy → select the Player, then Inspector → Rigidbody 2D → Gravity Scale. Set it to 1 while the game is running and watch the character drop. Then try 0.2 and describe the difference out loud.
  3. Game view → stop Play, then Inspector → Gravity Scale: it is back to 0. Inspector edits made during Play are thrown away on Stop (1.2) — which is why the cave's gravity has to end up in code.
  4. Hierarchy → open the Overworld scene — the top-down hub — select its Player, and set Inspector → Gravity Scale to 1. Game view → press Play: you have just broken the hub. Write down what it cost, then set it back to 0.
  5. Hierarchy → back in the cave, select the Player and read Inspector → Player Controller. There is a leftover override called Is Platformer that no field in your script matches yet. Leave it — step 1 of the walkthrough below is about it.
  6. Once the walkthrough is done — Hierarchy → the Player standing in the cave, Inspector → Player Controller → Is Platformer, and tick it. Confirm the Overworld's copy is unticked, then Game view → press Play in both: the cave falls, the hub does not.
In the Code ~30 min

Four calls do all of it — the key, the gravity, the push, and the instrument that proves the push worked:

APIWhat it isWhat you getWhat it costs
Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) A key check that is true for exactly one frame. A press you can act on once. Nothing — unless you reach for Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space) instead. That one is true every frame the key is held, and a jump built on it is a jetpack.
rb.gravityScale A multiplier on the project gravity, set per body. Down, at whatever strength you choose. It means nothing on a Kinematic body. A body that ignores gravity still accepts a push, and then rises forever.
rb.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse) One instant change in momentum. A parabola that gravity finishes for you. Mass divides into it, so retuning mass retunes every jump. Drop the force mode and the push becomes a dribble instead of a jump.
rb.linearVelocity How fast the body is travelling, in units per second. A number you can read to watch the arc. Reading it is free. Writing it erases whatever vertical motion was already there — a platform lift, a knockback, a bounce.
Architectural specification: the gravity and the flick.
  • Where does the cave's gravity get turned on — a field default, Start(), or every frame? Say what breaks at the other two.
  • Which key did you choose, and is the check Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) or Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space)? Say what holding the key for two seconds does under each.
  • Is your jump force a serialized field or a number typed into the condition? Does its name say force or speed — and what does the name make the next reader believe?
  • How do you know the jump worked? Name what you would print, and what it proves.

Socratic: Gravity Is a Number You Own

  1. Real gravity is a constant of the universe. Unity ships it as an Inspector field you can set per object. Why would an engine make a law of physics editable?
  2. Same Player prefab, same script, two worlds: the hub needs Gravity Scale 0 and the cave needs it above 0. Where should that difference live — the prefab, the scene, or the script — and what does each choice cost the next person who places a Player?
  3. A Kinematic body ignores gravity, forces and mass entirely. Set Body Type to Kinematic in the cave, and what would your jump code have to do instead to look like a jump?
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I make the player jump in the cave?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. There is no Jump() in Unity, and nobody is going to give you one. What is left after the editor half is two fields, one gated gravity line, one key check, one push and a way to see that it worked. The push is where every mistake in this lesson happens.

Step 1Declare how hard the flick is, and which world you are in

Two fields in the class body beside moveSpeed, for the same reason moveSpeed is there: they are numbers and facts a person tunes, not values you bury inside a condition.

    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;

    [SerializeField] private bool isPlatformer = false;
  1. 1How hard the flick is. Named jumpForce because that is what the call takes - a force - so no reader mistakes it for the speed the character leaves the ground at.A starting guess, not a value. The number that makes a jump feel right is found in the tuning lab at the bottom of this page. And a force is divided by mass before it becomes motion, so the height 7f buys depends on the mass the Inspector shows.
  2. 3Which world this Player woke up in. false is the default, so a Player in any scene nobody has ticked keeps the top-down behaviour it has had since 2.1.The name is not free, and you can check why. Click the cave's Player and look at PlayerController: the scene has carried an override called Is Platformer since before this course existed - a leftover from the version of this script that shipped with the project. Unity stores overrides by field name, so this spelling picks the tick back up where inCave would lose it. Check the box either way.

Step 2Turn gravity on once, in a method that runs once

The body lookup you already do in Start() is unchanged. What is new is one line underneath it, wrapped in the flag.

        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        if (isPlatformer)
        {
            body.gravityScale = 1f;
        }
  1. 1The reference you already cache here - the body about to be given a gravity scale. GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>() finds the component on the same GameObject as this script.Leave it exactly where it is. A lookup in Start() happens once; the same lookup inside Update() would run every frame for a reference that never changes. That is the rule you have followed since you first cached anything.
  2. 3The gate. Read it as "if this Player is standing in the cave". It is the only thing separating the two worlds.Read once, in a method that runs once. Start() is the once-only setup method from 1.3, and a fact about the scene belongs there.
  3. 5The whole of turning gravity on. body.gravityScale is the Rigidbody2D property behind the Inspector field you have been reading all year, and 1f means "the project gravity, undiluted".Why this is code and not a number in the Inspector. You could set the cave copy to 1 by hand and write nothing - but that number is invisible to a reader of your script, and it has to be repeated on every new Player anyone places.

Step 3Notice the press, and spend it in one line

Four lines at the bottom of the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4 - after your movement and your animation lines, where the frame already knows what the player is doing.

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        }
  1. 1Input is the class from 1.4, KeyCode.Space names the key, and Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) is true on the single frame the key goes down.The wrong key check fails in the loudest way there is. Without Down, the check is true on every frame the key is held, so half a second of holding Space applies thirty pushes and the character leaves the top of the level. The jump looks broken; the condition is. And the check belongs in Update(): FixedUpdate() is the physics clock, which can run several times in one frame or skip frames, so a one-frame press can be counted twice or missed.
  2. 3The flick. Vector2.up is (0, 1) - straight up - scaled by the field from step 1. Read the call as a sentence: add a force, upward, of this size, as an impulse.The second argument is the whole lesson, and leaving it out is the classic bug. With ForceMode2D.Impulse this is one hit, spent at the next physics step. Without it the default is a force that keeps applying while the calls keep coming - and since this line sits inside a check true on exactly one frame, you get a dribble so small the character twitches and settles. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and "my jump does nothing" is what you write in the group chat.

Step 4Prove the arc in the Console, then take the print out

There is no UI for vertical velocity, so the Console is your instrument. One temporary print, at the bottom of Update() where every frame runs.

        Debug.Log("v.y = " + body.linearVelocity.y);
// Delete the print before you move on
  1. 1At the bottom of Update(), outside the key block, with no condition on it. body.linearVelocity is how fast the body is travelling, read instead of written, and .y is the half a jump cares about.That number is the parabola. It jumps to a peak when you press Space, shrinks as gravity takes it back, crosses zero at the top of the arc, and grows negative all the way down. The apex is not a place in your code - it is the frame this number passes through nothing.
  2. 2An instrument, not a feature. A print left here fills the Console with a thousand lines a minute and buries the next real error under them.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Two differences are worth naming, and neither is a mistake. First the shape: the walkthrough wrote the push inline inside the key check, and this file gives it a method called Jump() - the same line, with a name you can point at when a ground check asks what a jump is allowed to do. Second the gravity line: this file decides the number for both worlds with a ternary where the walkthrough only wrote it for one. Your key, your number and the names of your own methods are yours.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerController.cs - the jump, complete.
// Everything from 1.4 to 4.4 (input, movement, animation, coins, health)
// stays exactly as you wrote it. The flag, the gravity line, the key check
// and the push are the whole of what is new.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;      // your number
    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;      // how hard the flick is
    [SerializeField] private bool isPlatformer = false; // which world did I wake up in?

    private Rigidbody2D body;

    void Start()
    {
        // Looked up once, never inside Update() - the rule from 2.1.
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        // Decided once, for both worlds. The hub's 0 is written here rather
        // than inherited from the prefab, so the decision is visible to
        // anyone reading this file instead of only to the Inspector.
        body.gravityScale = isPlatformer ? 1f : 0f;
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... input, movement and animation, from 1.4 to 4.4 ...

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            Jump();
        }
    }

    // The whole jump. One impulse, and gravity spends it over the next half
    // second - which is why there is nothing here about coming back down.
    private void Jump()
    {
        body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
}
Build Lab: Tune It ~15 min

Change one number at a time and write one sentence of feel for each, in a file you keep. Three knobs, and the third one is the interesting one.

KnobTry
jumpForce — Inspector → Player Controllerhalf, then double
Gravity Scale — Inspector → Rigidbody 2D0.2, then 1, then 4
Mass — Inspector → Rigidbody 2D1, then 5 — watch the jump and the fall

Then walk back through the cave mouth into the hub and jump there. It should do nothing — and if it does something, read Gravity Scale on the Overworld's Player before you read your code.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break "make the player jump" into its parts before you write any code, and name the earlier lesson you lifted each one from
  • Say why the cave needs gravity on and the hub needs it off, and where that difference is decided
  • Write a key check that fires on one frame, and say what the held-key version does instead
  • Explain what ForceMode2D.Impulse changes about the push, and what happens without it
  • Read body.linearVelocity.y in the Console and point at the apex without a UI
  • Commit and push
